This series uses two public datasets to answer questions that pharmacies and pharmaceutical and distribution teams ask. "Monitoring reimbursement changes and demand", published as one report on 2026-11-24, was split into the pages below on 2026-11-27. The full Korean version of this overview is [here](../../../ko/posts/2026-11-pharm-data-series/index.qmd).

| Question | Data | Page |
|---|---|---|
| (Stock value) How many days ahead can a pharmacy know about a price cut, and how small is it? Can announced cuts be trusted? | HIRA reimbursement list 2022-01 to 2025-12 | [Only in 2024 could most price cuts be seen a month ahead](../2026-11-benefit-change-lead/index.qmd) |
| Which way is demand for each ingredient heading? How well can six months ahead be forecast? | NHIS drug usage statistics 2018-01 to 2025-12 | [Ingredient prescription demand](../2026-11-drug-demand-forecast/index.qmd) |
| How were those numbers checked? | Same data | [Demand forecasting technical note](../2026-11-drug-demand-tech-note/index.qmd) |

## Does combining the two datasets help? {#list-price}

**Adding reimbursement-list price information to demand forecasts did not show an improvement.** With the price changes visible in the list at forecast time, unit-price forecast error was 0.0186 vs 0.0217, about 15% lower, but p = 0.252 could not be told apart from chance, nor from forecasts with the timing deliberately shifted. For prescription volume, the test could not even detect a deliberately injected 20% effect, so it could not measure an effect. The median pass-through from list price change to claimed unit price was only 0.55. The series therefore uses the reimbursement list for price and suspension alerts and the usage statistics for demand. The criteria were fixed before results were seen; the table is in the [technical note](../2026-11-drug-demand-tech-note/index.qmd#list-price-test).

## Ground rules

- A future date in the remarks is an **announcement**, not a change. Pages say "a cut was announced" or "realization rate 99.96%", never "the price was cut".
- Price changes and prescription volume are compared only as before-and-after changes and associations, not as causes.
- Demand forecasts are national and per ingredient, not order quantities for a pharmacy or product.
- No savings or incentive amounts are computed.
- The data contain no product-level sales, pharmacy purchases or stock, wholesale distribution, or planned delisting dates.

## Next analyses {#next}

The order follows the pharmacy pain points in the Korean overview, weighted by how much information can reduce them and by what is coming (re-evaluation of listed drugs from 2027). "Possible now" means the public data already in hand are enough.

| # | Analysis | Pain point | Why | Possible now? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **How far ahead can a cut be known:** split cuts into noted cuts, bulk cuts and other cuts without a note; measure the share visible in the list at least a month ahead and the size of cuts (won and percent) | Stock value | Answers "we only learn days before, so we give up checking" and "1-won cuts are a loss we just absorb" with numbers | **Done (2026-11-27).** Seeing a cut a month ahead happened mostly in 2024 (80.8%; 0–0.35% in other years). Bulk cuts were known 4–13 days ahead through notices and association guidance; 19.6% of the 2026-01 actual-transaction-price cuts were 1 won. [2nd edition](../2026-11-benefit-change-lead/index.qmd#lead) |
| 2 | **Re-evaluation exposure map:** describe which products were cut in the 2023-09 base-requirement re-evaluation, and count products in today's list with similar characteristics | Stock value | The pain point expected to worsen fastest | Possible now (descriptive). There has been essentially one bulk re-evaluation, so no predictive model |
| 3 | **Supply-vulnerability map:** trend of listed products and companies per ingredient, delistings, suspensions and price-ceiling increases, to find ingredients with few substitutes | Procurement | The part of shortages that public data can address is "can it be substituted?" | Map possible now. Matching with actual shortages needs supply-interruption reports; until then results are "vulnerability candidates" |
| 4 | **Delisting, suspension and unsellable stock:** was there a signal before a product left the list or was suspended, and how many same-ingredient substitutes existed then | Stock value | Can warn about stock that may become unreturnable | Possible now. Planned delisting dates are not in the data |
| 5 | **Reported shortage cases:** did ingredient prescriptions change sharply around reported shortages | Procurement | Links field complaints to data | Conditional. Ingredients with two or fewer companies are suppressed in the usage statistics; used as validation cases for #3 |
| 6 | **Leading signals for winter respiratory and antibiotic demand:** do search indices, paediatric care flows and the calendar move ahead of prescription increases | Procurement | Fever-reducer and antibiotic shortages cluster in winter and overlap with the largest forecast errors | In progress. Results are leading correlations, not causes or shortage forecasts |
| 7 | **Long-term prescribing trend:** volume per claim by province, care-institution type and age | Dispensing | Long prescriptions add to stock and consumable burden | Possible but the indicator is weak: volume is in product units, not days supplied |

Warehouse-style pharmacies and dispensing fees per pharmacy are not covered: there are no pharmacy- or area-level data.

**Other candidates:** ingredient unit price around changes in the generic-substitution list, ingredient markets around patent expiry and generic entry, prescription flows by province and facility type, how combining strengths and forms affects forecast error, and an example of a single pharmacy alert built from the change log.
